- dataviz: Use this skill whenever you are about to create ANY chart, graph, plot, dashboard, or data visualization, in ANY output medium — an HTML or React artifact, inline SVG, plotting code in any library (matplotlib, plotly, d3, Recharts, …), an image/PNG you will render and upload, or a chart shared into Slack. Read it BEFORE writing the first line of chart code, choosing chart colors, building a stat tile / meter / KPI row, or laying out a dashboard. Produces visualizations that read as one system — elegant, accessible, consistent in light and dark — using a brand-neutral placeholder palette you swap for your own. Teaches a design-system-agnostic method: a form heuristic, a color formula with a runnable validator, mark specs, and interaction rules. A validated default palette is documented in `references/palette.md` — swap that file's values for your brand's. Triggers on: "chart", "graph", "plot", "data viz", "visualization", "dashboard", "analytics", "visualize data", "categorical colors", "sequential / diverging palette", "stat tile", "sparkline", "heatmap", "legend", "axis", "tooltip", "chart colors", "color by series".
- update-config: Use this skill to configure the Claude Code harness via settings.json. Automated behaviors ("from now on when X", "each time X", "whenever X", "before/after X") require hooks configured in settings.json - the harness executes these, not Claude, so memory/preferences cannot fulfill them. Also use for: permissions ("allow X", "add permission", "move permission to"), env vars ("set X=Y"), hook troubleshooting, or any changes to settings.json/settings.local.json files. Examples: "allow npm commands", "add bq permission to global settings", "move permission to user settings", "set DEBUG=true", "when claude stops show X". For simple settings like theme/model, suggest the /config command.
- keybindings-help: Use when the user wants to customize keyboard shortcuts, rebind keys, add chord bindings, or modify ~/.claude/keybindings.json. Examples: "rebind ctrl+s", "add a chord shortcut", "change the submit key", "customize keybindings".
- verify: Verify that a code change actually does what it's supposed to by exercising it end-to-end and observing behavior — drive the affected flow, not just tests or typecheck. Run before committing nontrivial changes; bootstraps this repo's project verify skill if none exists yet. Don't invoke it on a diff that only touches tests, docs, or other code with no runtime surface to drive (a change to product source always has one) — there's nothing to observe.
- code-review: Review the current diff for correctness bugs and reuse/simplification/efficiency cleanups at the given effort level (low/medium: fewer, high-confidence findings; high→max: broader coverage, may include uncertain findings). Pass --comment to post findings as inline PR comments, or --fix to apply the findings to the working tree after the review.
- simplify: Review the changed code for reuse, simplification, efficiency, and altitude cleanups, then apply the fixes. Quality only — it does not hunt for bugs; use /code-review for that.

content.text: I ran ~20,100 probes attacking the rule from the length-and-boundary angle. The core predicate survived every one. I did find two false claims in the rule's supporting evidence/methodology, plus silences worth resolving.

counterexamples.predictedByRule: Unobservable — the rule states "DEL-range not tested (unreachable via argv along with NUL)", so it makes no verifiable claim about 0x7F.
counterexamples.actual: Fully observable and tested. Output = 1|0|1|0|0. First "://" is at index 2 == |scheme|, LINE3=1 and LINE5=0 confirm a clean parse, so scheme="a\x7F" was handed to is_scheme_valid and rejected. Also verified: "\x7F://host" => 1|0|1|0|0 (DEL at index 0), "a\x7Fb://host" => 1|0|1|0|0, and 0x7F at every index of schemes of length 1..24. Only 0x00 is genuinely unreachable through argv. The predicate's prediction (invalid) is correct; the rule's evidence statement is wrong.

counterexamples.input: a:://host  (bytes 61 3a 3a 2f 2f 68 6f 73 74) and a/://host, ab:://host, a:/://host, a//://host, a:b://host, a/b://host
counterexamples.predictedByRule: Unobservable/perturbed — the rule's methodology note says "S containing ':' or '/' shifts where the first \"://\" is found and thus truncates the scheme actually handed to is_scheme_valid", i.e. these probes cannot test ':' or '/' inside a scheme.
counterexamples.actual: All are clean, directly usable probes. For "a:://host" the first "://" is at index 2 == |"a:"|, output 1|0|1|0|0 with LINE3=1/LINE5=0 (host still parsed). Same for a/ (idx 2), ab: (idx 3), a:/ (idx 3), a// (idx 3), a:b (idx 3), a/b (idx 3) — all 1|0|1|0|0. So ':' and '/' inside a scheme ARE observable and ARE rejected. The only genuinely unobservable candidates are those containing the substring "://" (the split moves to the earlier occurrence) or containing '#'/'?' (stripped from the whole URL before the split).

input.correctedRule:
is_scheme_valid(s) is a pure function of the byte string s: no trimming, no case folding, no percent-decoding, no locale sensitivity, and no length limit.

fn is_scheme_valid(s: &[u8]) -> bool {
    if s.is_empty() { return false; }                    // empty => false
    if !s[0].is_ascii_alphabetic() { return false; }      // s[0] in 'A'..='Z' | 'a'..='z'
    for &c in &s[1..] {
        let ok = c.is_ascii_alphanumeric() || c == b'+' || c == b'-' || c == b'.';
        if !ok { return false; }
    }
    true
}

Equivalent byte-wise anchored regex: ^[A-Za-z][A-Za-z0-9+.-]*$   (note: must be anchored with \z / \0, not a Perl-style `$`, which would wrongly accept a trailing "\n" — e.g. scheme "a\n" is INVALID: "a\n://host" => 1|0|1|0|0).

CHARACTER CLASSES (verified byte-exhaustively, 0x01-0xFF, at index 0, 1, 2, 4, at every index of every length 1..24, and at indices 0, n/2, n-2, n-1 for n up to 131000):
- Index 0: valid only for the 52 bytes 0x41-0x5A and 0x61-0x7A. Invalid for every other byte 0x01-0xFF, including all C0 controls 0x01-0x1F, space 0x20, all punctuation 0x21-0x40 / 0x5B-0x60 / 0x7B-0x7E, DEL 0x7F, and all 128 high bytes 0x80-0xFF (no locale-dependent isalpha; behaves as pure "C"-locale ASCII; UTF-8 letters such as 0xC3 0xA9 are rejected).
- Indices >= 1: valid only for A-Z (0x41-0x5A), a-z (0x61-0x7A), 0-9 (0x30-0x39), '+' (0x2B), '-' (0x2D), '.' (0x2E). Invalid for everything else, explicitly including '_' 0x5F, '~' 0x7E, '%' 0x25, ':' 0x3A, '/' 0x2F, '*', '!', '=', ',', ';', '@', '$', '&', '\'', '(', ')', '[', ']', '^', '{', '|', '}', '<', '>', '"', '`', '\\', space, all C0 controls 0x01-0x1F, DEL 0x7F, and all 128 high bytes 0x80-0xFF.
- The index >= 1 rule is positionally uniform: no distinction between index 1, an interior index, and the final index; no "last character" exemption and no "last character" extra restriction. Trailing '+', '-', '.' are accepted ("a-", "a.", "a+", "a...", "a---", "a+++", and 'a' followed by 1..40 repetitions of '+'/'-'/'.' are all valid). A bad byte at index n-1 is rejected exactly as at index 0 or n/2, verified for n = 2..24 and n = 1000, 4096, 8192, 16384, 32768, 65536, 131000.

LENGTH BOUNDARIES:
- Minimum: length 0 => false; length 1 => true iff the single byte is an ASCII letter (all 255 single-byte schemes swept; only the 52 letters are valid).
- No maximum. Verified valid for all-'a' schemes of every length 1..140 and at 150, 200, 255, 256, 257, 300, 400, 511, 512, 513, 1000, 1023, 1024, 1025, 2047, 2048, 2049, 4095, 4096, 4097, 8191, 8192, 8193, 16383, 16384, 16385, 32768, 65535, 65536, 100000, 131000, and up to a full argv of 131071 bytes. 131072+ is not testable: Linux MAX_ARG_STRLEN (131072) rejects the exec, so the largest scheme observable through this driver is 131064 bytes ("scheme" + "://host"). No length limit exists within that entire observable range, and a single bad byte still flips the result at length 131000.
- 0x00 (NUL) cannot be delivered through argv, so is_scheme_valid's behavior on an embedded NUL is UNVERIFIABLE through this driver. Do not claim it either way. (0x7F/DEL, by contrast, IS reachable and IS invalid at every position.)

PURITY / CONTEXT INDEPENDENCE: LINE 2 depends only on the extracted scheme bytes. For each of 15 fixed schemes, the same LINE 2 value was produced across 17 structurally different suffixes ("://host", "://host/", "://host/a/b", "://host:80", "://host:99999", "://u:p@host", "://", ":///", "://[::1]:8080/x", "://host?q=1", "://host#f", "://host/a?b#c", "://   ", "://host/../.", "://:", "://@", "://a://b") — 0 distinct values within each scheme. Presence/absence of userinfo, port, path, query, fragment, IPv6 host, or a second "://" never changes LINE 2.

NO NORMALIZATION ON THIS PATH (all verified):
- No percent-decoding: "a%62c://host" => 1|0|1|0|0, "ht%74p://host" => 1|0|1|0|0, "%61%62://host" => 1|0|1|0|0, "%68ttp://host" => 1|0|1|0|0, "a%://host" => 1|0|1|0|0. ('%' is simply an invalid scheme byte.)
- No trim(): " http://host", "http ://host", "\thttp://host", "http\t://host", "  http  ://host", and the '\n', '\r', '\v', '\f' variants all give LINE 2 = 0. The raw input URL is not trimmed by parse() either.
- No case requirement and no known-scheme whitelist: "http", "HTTP", "HtTp", "a", "A", "z", "Z" all valid; "http+ssh", "a1+2-3.4" valid. Whether the implementation lowercases before checking is behaviorally indistinguishable through this interface (the character class is case-symmetric), so that is an implementation claim, not an observed fact.

CORRECT METHODOLOGY FOR RE-VERIFICATION (supersedes the original note, which was too restrictive): to observe is_scheme_valid(S), run S + "://host" and accept the probe only if (a) S contains neither '#' (0x23) nor '?' (0x3F) — those are stripped from the whole URL before the "://" split, e.g. "ab#://host" => 1|0|0|0|1|[ab] — and (b) index_of("://", S + "://host") == len(S), which holds for every S that does not contain "://" as a substring. Under this filter, S may freely contain ':' and '/'; those cases parse cleanly and are legitimately testable (all rejected). Confirm each probe with LINE3 == 1 and LINE5 == 0. Only S containing the literal substring "://" is unobservable.

CONSEQUENCE FOR THE DRIVER: when the input URL contains no "://", scheme() is "" and LINE 2 is 0 (the whole input becomes the path) — e.g. "example.com", "a", "a:", "a:/", "http:/example.com", "http%3A%2F%2Fhost" all give LINE 2 = 0. When the URL starts with "://", scheme() is "" and LINE 2 = 0.

~20,100 probes run against /workspace/dataset/test16_executable (perl harness at /tmp/lib.pl, drivers /tmp/t1.pl through /tmp/t11.pl). Every probe was compared programmatically against the predicate ^[A-Za-z][A-Za-z0-9+.-]*\z and simultaneously screened for a clean parse (LINE3==1 && LINE5==0) so that a perturbed split could never be mistaken for a scheme rejection.

THE PREDICATE ITSELF IS CONFIRMED — zero functional counterexamples. Breakdown:
- 171 length probes, all-'a' schemes, lengths 1..140 plus 33 larger values up to 131000: all valid, 0 mismatches.
- 510 probes: every byte 0x01-0xFF as a length-1 scheme and at index 1 of a length-2 scheme: 0 mismatches. (This is the length-2 boundary case where index 1 is simultaneously "first non-leading char" and "last char" — no off-by-one.)
- 11,400 probes: 38 distinct invalid bytes injected at every single index of schemes of length 1..24: 0 mismatches. This kills any off-by-one in the loop bounds (no skipped first-after-index-0, no skipped final char).
- 517 probes: digits and '+','-','.' at index 0 for lengths 1..12, 20, 31/32/33, 63/64/65, 127/128/129, 255/256/257, 1023/1024/1025 (all invalid); 'a' + 0..40 trailing '+'/'-'/'.' (all valid); 4096-byte schemes with a single '_' at the leading, trailing, and middle position.
- 5,880 randomized probes (seeded, reproducible): 3,000 over the full byte range 0x01-0xFF at lengths 1-9, and 2,880 over a 40-char boundary-heavy near-miss alphabet, both filtered for observability: 0 mismatches.
- 759 probes: every byte 0x01-0xFF at index 0, 2, and 4 of a length-5 scheme: 0 mismatches (rules out any positional dependency for high bytes/controls at interior vs terminal positions).
- 270 purity probes: 15 schemes x 17 suffix contexts, plus 15 structural edge probes.
- Length ceiling nailed down: valid at argv length 131071 (scheme 131064 bytes), exec fails at 131072 due to Linux MAX_ARG_STRLEN, not the library. "No length limit" is therefore verified across the entire range this driver can reach.

WHY 'corrected' RATHER THAN 'confirmed': the predicate is right, but two explicitly-stated evidence/methodology claims in the proposed rule are factually false and would mislead anyone re-verifying it, and three points were left silent. (1) "DEL-range not tested (unreachable via argv along with NUL)" is wrong — 0x7F is perfectly reachable via argv; I tested it at index 0, index 1, interior, and every index of lengths 1..24, and it is invalid everywhere. Only 0x00 is unreachable. (2) The note that a scheme containing ':' or '/' cannot be probed because the "://" split shifts is wrong for most such schemes — "a:", "a/", "ab:", "a:/", "a//", "a:b", "a/b" all yield first-"://" at exactly index |S| with a clean parse, so ':' and '/' inside schemes are directly verified invalid rather than merely inferred; only schemes containing the literal substring "://" are unobservable. (3) Silences now resolved: the observable length ceiling (131064 bytes, OS-imposed), the genuine unverifiability of NUL, and the fact that the "no lowercasing before the check" statement is an unobservable implementation claim (the class is case-symmetric). I also flag a trap for re-implementers: a Perl/PCRE-style unanchored-at-end `$` makes the stated regex wrongly accept a trailing "\n"; the binary rejects "a\n" (verified: "a\n://host" => 1|0|1|0|0), so the anchor must be \z.

No functional defect in the predicate was found despite a deliberate, exhaustive length-and-boundary attack.
